\chapter{Amicus, Pecunia, Medicus, Miles, Epistula}
\label{ch:la-urbani}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a friend, money, a doctor, a soldier and a letter — five words a Roman town could not be described without.}

The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[amīcus, amīcī]{amīcus — from the verb to love, and the word the bread lesson pointed at and did not give}

\label{lesson:LA-C51-amicus}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ibi} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hic} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sāl} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sciō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{viridis} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quid agis?} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{amīcus} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a friend}.\textquotedblright{}

The bread lesson traced \emph{pānis} to \textbf{companion} — the one you share bread with — and to \textquotedblleft{}the friendship-word every Romance daughter still shares.\textquotedblright{} This is that word, and it took forty-one chapters to arrive.

It is built straight onto \textbf{amō}, \textquotedblleft{}I love,\textquotedblright{} from the \emph{amō} lesson: a friend is simply one who is loved. And its negative is the interesting half. \textbf{In-amīcus} becomes \textbf{inimīcus}, \textquotedblleft{}not-friend,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{inimīcus} is English \textbf{enemy}. The most hostile word in the language is the friendliest one with two letters in front of it.

Spanish \emph{amigo}, Italian \emph{amico}, Portuguese \emph{amigo} and French \emph{ami} are all this word unchanged. English borrowed \textbf{amicable}, \textbf{amity} and \textbf{amiable} from it, and took \textbf{enemy} from its opposite by way of French.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{amīcus, amīcī}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb is \emph{amīcus} built on? (\emph{\textbf{Amō}}, I love.) What is \emph{inimīcus}, and what English word is it? (\textbf{Not-friend}; \emph{\textbf{enemy}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pecūnia, pecūniae]{pecūnia — and the cattle it is named after}

\label{lesson:LA-C51-pecunia}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{amīcus} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{iste} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mel} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ut valēs?} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{valeō} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pecūnia} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{money}.\textquotedblright{}

The word is a fossil of what wealth used to be. \textbf{Pecū} meant \textquotedblleft{}cattle,\textquotedblright{} and a Roman's \emph{pecūnia} was originally his livestock. When Rome began to strike coins it stamped an ox on them, and the name of the herd became the name of the money.

The English family is larger than it looks:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pecuniary} — to do with money, straight from \emph{pecūnia}.
  \item \textbf{impecunious} — having none.
  \item \textbf{peculiar} — from \emph{pecūlium}, the private property a Roman slave or son was allowed to keep. \textquotedblleft{}One's own\textquotedblright{} narrowed to \textquotedblleft{}odd\textquotedblright{} over the centuries.
  \item \textbf{fee} — a Germanic \textbf{cousin}, not a loan: Old English \emph{feoh} meant both cattle and property, from the same Proto-Indo-European root.
\end{itemize}

The same picture is behind English \textbf{capital}, from \emph{caput} — a head of cattle — and \emph{caput} is the first body word this book taught.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pecūnia, pecūniae}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{pecūnia} originally mean? (\textbf{Cattle}.) Is English \emph{fee} a cousin or a loan? (\textbf{A cousin}.) And which body word tells the same story? (\emph{\textbf{Caput}} — capital, a head of cattle.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[medicus, medicī]{medicus — from measuring, not from healing}

\label{lesson:LA-C51-medicus}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pecūnia} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ille} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lac} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{cōgitō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{salvē — quid agis? — valeō — valē} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quid tibi nōmen est? / mihi nōmen est...} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{medicus} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a doctor}.\textquotedblright{}

Not, as you might expect, from a word for healing. \textbf{Medicus} is from \emph{medeor}, \textquotedblleft{}I attend to,\textquotedblright{} and behind that is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*med-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to measure, to take the appropriate measures.\textquotedblright{} A doctor, to a Roman, is someone who works out the right amount.

The root spread widely on that meaning:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{meditate} — to measure a thing over in the mind.
  \item \textbf{moderate} and \textbf{modest} — kept within measure.
  \item \textbf{mete}, as in \textquotedblleft{}mete out\textquotedblright{} — an inherited English \textbf{cousin}, not a loan.
  \item \textbf{remedy} — \emph{re-} plus \emph{medeor}, attending to a thing again.
\end{itemize}

Every Romance language kept the word: Spanish \emph{médico}, Italian \emph{medico}, Portuguese \emph{médico}. English took \textbf{medicine}, \textbf{medical} and \textbf{medic} from the same family, and French gave us \textbf{medico} back as slang.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{medicus, medicī}

What does the root behind \emph{medicus} really mean? (\textbf{To measure}, to take the right measures.) Name two English words from it that are not about health. (\emph{\textbf{Moderate}}, \emph{\textbf{modest}}, \emph{\textbf{meditate}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mīles, mīlitis]{mīles — the noun every Latin narrative turns on}

\label{lesson:LA-C51-miles}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{medicus} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{is} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ōvum} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{legō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quid tibi nōmen est? / mihi nōmen est...} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{puerō nōmen est Mārcus / Mārcō} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mīles} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a soldier}.\textquotedblright{}

The noun a reader of Latin meets on the first page of almost any history, and one this book went fifty chapters without.

Note the shape: nominative \textbf{mīles}, genitive \textbf{mīlitis}. The \emph{-t-} that appears in the genitive is the real stem, and every English derivative is built on the genitive rather than the nominative — \textbf{military}, \textbf{militia}, \textbf{militant}, \textbf{militarise}. That is a general habit worth having: when an English word from Latin looks nothing like the Latin nominative, look at the genitive.

Where the word came from is \textbf{not settled}. The old suggestion is \emph{mille}, \textquotedblleft{}thousand\textquotedblright{} — a soldier as one of a thousand-strong unit — and it is a guess with no evidence behind it. Some scholars propose an Etruscan borrowing. Treat the etymology as \textbf{open}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mīles, mīlitis}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form do the English derivatives come from? (\textbf{The genitive}, \emph{mīlitis} — hence \emph{military}.) Is the etymology settled? (\textbf{No} — the \emph{mille} story is a guess.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[epistula, epistulae]{epistula — a Greek word Rome borrowed, and the thing Cicero wrote in his letters}

\label{lesson:LA-C51-epistula}



\begin{quote}
Six recalls before the new word, at growing distances. They are not decoration: each one is the retrieval window this book measures, and each names a word far enough back that saying it is work.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mīles} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ibi} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{piscis} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{intellegō} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from the same distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{puerō nōmen est Mārcus / Mārcō} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{volup est convēnisse} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, a second word from that far back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{epistula} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a letter}.\textquotedblright{}

The farewell lessons quoted \textbf{two} of Cicero's letters and never gave you the word for one. Here it is, and it is Greek: \emph{epistolē}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing sent \textbf{to} somebody,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{epi-} (\textquotedblleft{}to, upon\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{stellō} (\textquotedblleft{}I send\textquotedblright{}). Rome borrowed the object and the word together.

The same \emph{stellō} is inside \textbf{apostle} — \emph{apo-stolos}, \textquotedblleft{}one sent \textbf{away}\textquotedblright{} — so an epistle and an apostle are the same verb with opposite prefixes, which is why the letters of the apostles are called epistles twice over.

\textbf{scrībō}, from the verbs of mind, is the verb this noun needed. \emph{Epistulam scrībō}: \textquotedblleft{}I am writing a letter.\textquotedblright{} The verbs of mind gave you the writing and the \emph{propediem} lesson gave you the reading, and this is the thing itself.
\end{cousinweb}
